analytic.title: Holistic Schedulability Analysis of a Fault-Tolerant Real-Time Distributed Run-time Support*

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: The feasibility test of a hard real-time system must not only take into account the temporal behavior of the application tasks but also the behavior of the run-time support in charge of executing applications. This paper is devoted to the schedulability analysis of a run-time support for distributed dependable hard real-time applications. In contrast to previous works that consider rather simple run-time supports (e.g. a real-time kernel made of a simple tick scheduler and an unreliable communication protocol), our work deals with a complex run-time support with fault-tolerance capabilities and made of multiple tasks that invoke each other.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Essentially for economic reasons, a new trend in the design of dependable hard real-time systems is to rely on Commercial Off-The-Shelf (COTS) components (hardware and operating system). COTS hardware and operating systems are generally not designed for dependable applications. Using them in order to execute hard real-time applications with dependability requirements means that fault-tolerance mechanisms must be implemented in a middleware layer on top of the operating system. As a consequence, the overall complexity of the run-time support is increased compared to a run-time support without dependability requirements.

The feasibility test of a hard real-time system must not only take into account the temporal behavior of the application tasks, but also the behavior of the run-time support in charge of executing them. This task is simple when the run-time support is small (e.g. a real-time kemel made of a simple tick scheduler and an unreliable communication protocol), but becomes more complex when it includes elaborate functions such as fault-tolerance mechanisms.

This paper is devoted to the schedulability analysis of a run-time support for distributed dependable hard real-time applications, through an adaptation of the distributed system arbitrary deadline analysis developed by Tindell [8] for fixed priority scheduling. This (Highly Available Distributed Embedded System) [ 11 was developed at the IRISA research center in Rennes, France, within the framework of a cooperation with the French department of defense (DGA) and Dassault-Aviation. Its objective is to execute applications in a predictable and reliable manner on top of COTS components (hardware and operating system). Two approaches can be used to obtain task response times in distributed real-time systems. On one hand, one can simultaneously consider the application tasks and the run-time support tasks. On the other hand, the run-time support tasks can be considered separately; the knowledge of the system worst-case load scenario (e.g. worst-case arrival law of application tasks) is then used to compute the run-time support tasks response time. We have selected this second approach, because it allows to use a scheduling test for the application tasks different from the test for the run-time support tasks.

Single processor schedulability analysis for fixed priority tasks has received considerable attention. In the past ten years, the original fixed priority analysis [4] has been considerably extended, relaxing many of the assumptions of the original computation model (e.g. [3]). Single processor analysis for fixed priority has been also extended for network schedulability analysis (e.g. [7]) and for distributed system analysis (e.g. [SI). Several studies [8, 5, 2, 61 have considered the costs of a run-time support in the feasibility tests: [5, 2, 61 consider the influence of interrupts on the feasibility tests (static scheduling for the first reference, and dynamic priorities for the last two ones). The work of Tindell and Clark [8] deals with the schedulability analysis of a distributed system with tasks that communicate through message passing. In this work, the run-time support is rather simple: it is made of a tick scheduler and a simple unreliable TDMA communication procotol.

The contribution of this paper is to apply the arbitrary deadline analysis developed by Tindell [8] to compute the response times for the tasks of a run-time support for distributed dependable hard real-time applications. In contrast to previous works that consider rather simple systems, our work deals with a complex run-time support that incorporates fault-tolerance mechanisms, and which is made of multiple tasks that invoke each other.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. We present the HADES run-time support and detail how it schedules and executes tasks in section 2. Then, we compute the response times of the run-time support tasks (section 3). We conclude in section 4. Appendix A gives an exhaustive list of the runtime support tasks.
2 Run-time support

div.head: Architecture
div.p: Computations are distributed across several sites connected by a network. A site is made of a processor, a memory, a clock, and various interfaces (including a network interface, sensors, actuators). Resources (e.g. hardware resources, memory segments) can be shared between computations at a given site. Interrupts can come either from the clock or from the sensors.

div.head: Task model
div.p: Every task is modeled through a directed acyclic graph a node, called an EU (Elementary Unit), models a computation local to a site; an edge models a precedence relation between two nodes. A precedence relation is called local (resp. remote) when its EUs are assigned to the same site (resp. different sites).

An EU can either be a CodeEU (Code Elementary Unit), i.e. a blocking-free computation, or a SysEU (System Call Elementary Unit), i.e. the request of a service of the run- time support (e.g. reading the system clock). Direct calls to the underlying real-time kernel are not allowed for the application tasks. An EU uses input variables and computes output variables. Two EUs from the same graph can be located on different sites (tasks are distributed). A simple example of distributed task is given below.

div.head: Overview of the HADES run-time support
div.p: The HADES run-time support is a middleware layer running on top of a COTS real-time kernel. The run-time support is in charge of providing a set of services which can be called by applications thanks to SysEUs. The run-time support is also in charge of controlling the tasks' execution: it is implicitly called at specific points during the execution of tasks, namely:

1. Activation of tasks, to achieve the operations required between a task arrival (time when the task is logically able to run) and its release (time when it is inserted in the run-queues) ; Validation of precedence relations (a precedence relation from a to b is validated if the execution of a does not prevent b from executing anymore, i.e. if the execution of a is finished or the site of a is stopped) :
Termination of task executions, to free the resources used by task executions.

In addition, the run-time support is executed concurrently with application tasks to handle interrupts, and to achieve treatments which are asynchronous with regard to application tasks (detection of sites stops or starts, clock synchronization, polling of network communication buffers).
The run-time support is decomposed into two software layers:

A high level layer, named the services layer. Every service is modeled according to the task model shown in the previous paragraph. The service layer comprises a time sewice, whose purpose is to launch periodic tasks, and a set of fault-tolerant distributed services (5 2.3.1 to 2.3.4). Every service is made of several tasks. Some of them are entry points for the run-time support, and can be called thanks to SysEUs. For instance, the Sy-sEU returning the current system time is a call to task GetClock of the time service. To avoid any confusion, in the following an application task is named AppTask, and a run-time support task is named a RTSTask.

A low level layer, named dispatcher. The dispatcher implements a fixed-priority HFO scheduler for RTSZasks, while AppZasks can have their own scheduling algorithm, which is implemented by a scheduling service made of a set of RTSTasks (twolevel scheduling). The dispatcher maintains a priority- ordered set of run-queues containing the EUs of the tasks for which the execution is in progress. EU a has priority over EU b if a is in a run-queue with a higher priority than the one of b or if a is before b in the same run-queue. At any time, the eligible EU with the highest priority is executed. AppTasks scheduled by a given scheduling algorithm are associated with a fixed range of priorities.

The dispatcher controls the execution of the non distributed tasks (their activation, the validation of their precedence relations, and the termination of their executions), while distributed tasks are managed by a distributed execution control service (two-level execution control). The tasks of the distributed execution control service are called by the 'For flexibility reasons, services have been designed so that each of them can be replaced by another service with the same intehce but different properties [I]. Our run-time support comes with different versions of the multicast, failure detection and scheduling services. Only one service of each class is considered in the following.

The dispatcher also provides a small set of system calls. These calls are made thanks to SysEUs and are reserved for run-time support tasks, except for the Invocation system call which is used by application tasks to call services of the service layer. The system calls of the dispatcher are: Invocation: Call zero, one or several tasks (invocation mode = synchronous or asynchronous).
setclock: Update the dispatcher clock. ctrlRunQueue: Family of system calls used to update the run-time support run-queues. ctrlExec: Family of system calls used to control task execution.

There are two major differences between App Tasks and RTSTasks. First, the graph of App-Tasks is distributed (two EUs can be assigned to different sites), while the graph of RTS-Tasks is not. Second, App-Tasks have no direct access to the site hardware and to the real-time kemel, and are restricted to use the abstractions of the run-time support (resources, precedence relations, task invocation) to interact with one another.

A task (RTSTask or AppTask) is released either due to an interrupt (e.g., interrupt generated by a sensor) or because it is called by another task. In the latter case, the call can be either synchronous (the caller is blocked) or asynchronous. There is no code executed in interrupt handlers: rather, an interrupt handler only releases the task in charge of handling the interrupt. At a higher level of abstraction, App Tasks can be classified into two categories: 0 sensor-triggered App-Tasks, whose arrivals are triggered by a sensor each time it triggers an interrupt to indicate that data can be read;
the time-triggered AppTasks, that are called periodically by a task of the time service, which is triggered by the clock interrupt.
We now detail the functionalities of the services which are required for the schedulability analysis of the run-time support. Details can be found in [ 13.

div.head: Failure detection and reliable multicast
div.p: The failure detection service is in charge of detecting site failures, allowing fail-free sites to determine on the set of failed and operational sites (sites are assumed to be failsilent). It ensures the well-known properties of real-time A-timeliness, vivacity and integrity.

The multicast service is concerned with the (timebounded) transmission of messages to a set of sites despite link omissions (we assume the existence of an upper bound on the number of successive network omissions, as well as an upper bound on the network latency). It ensures the well-known properties of A-timeliness, validity, integrity agreement and virtual synchrony and delivers messages according to causal ordering. To multicast a message m, a RTS-Task task i synchronously calls a task of the reliable multicast service running on the local site (named mcastSend), which simply inserts m into the output communication buffer, managed in FIFO ordering. A periodic task, named mcastBg, is used to send the messages of the output communication buffer and to call asynchronously the tasks in charge of handling the messages in the input communication buffer. mcastBg also implements the failure detection service.

div.head: Clock synchronization
div.p: The clock synchronization service is concerned with keeping the sites clocks close from one another (the well-known properties of precision and accuracy are ensured). The protocol we have implemented is an adaptation of the algorithm of Lundelius and Lynch [9] to deal with a network with a bounded number of successive omissions instead of a reliable network as assumed in the original algorithm.

div.head: Distributed execution control
div.p: The distributed execution control service is made of a set of tasks, invoked when a distributed task is released or one of its EUs finishes. The above figure depicts the failure-free execution of a sensor-triggered AppTask (named i, which is the task taken in example in 3 2.2) made up of four EUs located on sites SI to s3.

A task of the distributed execution control service, named dstrActS sends a message to RTS-Tasks dstrActSD on sites SI, s2 and s3, where the successors of EU a are located. On these sites, RTS-Task dstrActSD, which is a proxy for task dstrActS, uses a system call of the ctrlExec family to allocate the execution resources required for the execution of i. Task dstrTerm is released at the end of the execution of each EU e; it sends a message to its proxy dstrTermD on every site where a successor of e is located (on the example, RTSTask dstrTerm of site s3 sends a message to site s2). On a given site, RTSTask dstrTermD validates the precedence relations which result from an EU put on a remote site thanks to a system call of the ctrlExec family.

div.head: Scheduling
div.p: The scheduling service is concemed with the selection of the order in which the EUs of AppTasks are to be inserted into the run-queues. Every scheduling service provides two tasks: task schedAct is released when a distributed task arrives; task schedTerni is released when an EU terminates its execution. The purpose of these two tasks is to update the dispatcher run-queues, using system calls of the ctrl-RunQueue family, according to a specific scheduling algorithm. One scheduling algorithm we have implemented is an extension to distributed tasks of the static planning-based scheduling algorithm of Xu and Parnas [ 101. In this scheduling service, schedAct simply inserts EUs in the run-queues according to a schedule computed off-line, and schedTerm simply removes from the run-queues the EU that has just finished its execution,

div.head: Tindell's results
div.p: A task is an infinite sequence of executions of a sequential program. Every task i is assigned a priority pr ,. We note hp(i) the set of tasks of higher priority than task i assigned to the same processor. Priorities are assumed to be unique, and at any time the task with the highest priority executes. For each arrival, a task i may execute a bounded amount of computation C,. Each task is periodic (resp. sporadic), i.e. there is an exact (resp. a minimal) delay P, between successive arrivals of task i. Each task i may lock/unlock semaphores according to the priority ceiling protocol or equivalent so that the longest time that task i could wait spend blocked by a lower priority task is bounded by a constant Bi.

div.head: Holistic analysis
div.p: The scheduling equations (equations 5, 8 and 10) are mutually dependent. For example, for RTSTusk i / , , Ji/. can depend on bm, with m sent by RTS-Tusk jfSt. So, b, depends on ri,s,, which can depend on RTS-Tusk kl, which has a higher priority than if,. Nevertheless, the equations used to compute ri have a solution, as shown by Tindell in [SI, because all the used scheduling equations are monotonic in window size w, response time, and release jitter. To find the solution, we adopt the solution proposed by Tindell: all the release jitters are considered null, which permits to compute a first estimation of response times and then of release jitters, and so on, until each response time converges, which is guaranteed if the system is not overloaded.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: In this paper, we have computed the response times of a complex run-time support tasks using a holistic approach, which is an adaptation of the distributed system arbitrary deadline analysis developed by Tindell for fixed priority scheduling. To be able to use Tindell's analysis, most tasks of the run-time support have been designed as periodic or sporadic tasks. For example, network management is achieved through periodic polling of the network buffer rather than using interrupts. For the remaining tasks (e.g. the task executed when a distributed task arrives), an artifice (transformation of tasks with an unknown arrival law into n sporadic tasks) has been used. Several extensions of the original analysis have been required to analyze our runtime support: extension to tasks that invoke other ones and extension to tasks with identical priorities, which were not supported in the original analysis. . dstrActS -mcastSend
